metadata.title: Self-reported teaching effectiveness and job satisfaction among teachers: the role of subject matter and other demographic variables

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a convenience sample of 173 Iranian teachers (English and non-English) recruited from specific cities and workplaces (public high schools and private language centers). The manuscript reports questionnaire administration and exclusion of incomplete responses, but it does not describe the use of any complex survey design weights or replicate-weight procedures. Because the analysis relies on standard nonparametric and correlational tests (e.g., Mann–Whitney U, Spearman correlation) rather than ILSA-style PV-based achievement modeling, there is no PV/scaling framework to weight. As a result, no sampling weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) is documented, and the weighting strategy is effectively not applicable/unspecified for this dataset.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are self-reported Likert-type job satisfaction scores and self-rated teaching effectiveness scores from teacher questionnaires, not cognitive achievement scales with PVs. Missing data handling is described at the analysis stage: questionnaires that were not filled out completely were excluded, which corresponds to listwise deletion. Therefore, PV and missing-data strategy are not part of an ILSA PV framework in this study.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Convenience sample of 173 Iranian teachers (English and non-English) from Urmia, Khoy, Andimeshk, and Tehran. Participants completed translated questionnaires; 200 questionnaires were distributed (60 online, 140 in person) and those not filled out completely were excluded. The final analytic sample therefore consists of complete responses meeting the study’s questionnaire completion requirements.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS-style teacher survey (Iranian convenience sample; no ILSA cycle/grade/domain)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Spearman correlation (job satisfaction vs experience): r = 0.040, sig > 0.05 (N=104). Mann–Whitney U for gender difference: Asymp. Sig. (2-tailed) = 0.374 (Table 7). Independent samples t-test for subject matter difference: sig > 0.05 (Table 8). Mann–Whitney U for employment status difference: Asymp. Sig. (2-tailed) = 0.474 (Table 9).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS-style teacher survey data from an Iranian convenience sample, the study leveraged Gender, Subject matter, Employment status, and Teaching experience to analyze job satisfaction among English teachers, finding that none of these background characteristics showed a statistically significant association with job satisfaction. This indicates that, in this context, teacher job satisfaction may be relatively stable across these demographic/workplace differences, suggesting policy efforts should target broader working conditions rather than only demographic subgroups.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS-style teacher survey (Iranian convenience sample; no ILSA cycle/grade/domain)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Spearman correlation (job satisfaction vs experience): r = -0.004, sig = 0.971 (N=69). Mann–Whitney U for gender difference: Asymp. Sig. (2-tailed) = 0.374 (Table 7). Independent samples t-test for subject matter difference: sig > 0.05 (Table 8). Mann–Whitney U for employment status difference: Asymp. Sig. (2-tailed) = 0.474 (Table 9).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS-style teacher survey data from an Iranian convenience sample, the study leveraged Gender, Subject matter, Employment status, and Teaching experience to analyze job satisfaction among non-English teachers, finding no statistically significant relationship between job satisfaction and teaching experience and no significant differences by gender or employment status. This indicates that, for non-English teachers in this sample, job satisfaction is not meaningfully differentiated by these observable background factors, implying that interventions may need to focus on workplace and support conditions rather than demographic targeting.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS-style teacher survey (Iranian convenience sample; no ILSA cycle/grade/domain)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Spearman correlation between job satisfaction and teaching effectiveness: rho = 0.628, sig = 0.000 (N=104) (Table 11).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS-style teacher survey data from an Iranian convenience sample, the study leveraged job satisfaction (and examined background variables) to predict teaching effectiveness among English teachers, finding a statistically significant positive correlation (Spearman rho = 0.628). This indicates that strengthening teacher job satisfaction may be associated with higher self-reported teaching effectiveness, though the cross-sectional correlational design means causality cannot be inferred.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS-style teacher survey (Iranian convenience sample; no ILSA cycle/grade/domain)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Spearman correlation between job satisfaction and teaching effectiveness: rho = 0.288, sig = 0.017 (N=69) (Table 12).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS-style teacher survey data from an Iranian convenience sample, the study leveraged job satisfaction (and examined background variables) to predict teaching effectiveness among non-English teachers, finding a statistically significant positive correlation (Spearman rho = 0.288). This indicates that improving job satisfaction may align with better self-reported teaching effectiveness for non-English teachers as well, while the non-causal correlational evidence limits policy claims about direction of effects.

data.outcome_summary: This Heliyon study used a convenience sample of 173 Iranian teachers (104 English teachers and 69 non-English teachers) and analyzed self-reported job satisfaction (Lester Teacher Job Satisfaction Questionnaire; 66 Likert items) and self-rated teaching effectiveness (Kulsum Teacher Effectiveness Scale; 60 items rated 1–10). The study reports no statistically significant associations between job satisfaction and teaching experience for either group (English: r=0.040, p>0.05; non-English: r=-0.004, p=0.971) and no significant gender or employment-status differences in job satisfaction (Mann–Whitney U p>0.05; Table 7 and Table 9). However, it finds a positive relationship between job satisfaction and teaching effectiveness for English teachers (Spearman rho=0.628, p<0.01) and a smaller but significant positive relationship for non-English teachers (rho=0.288, p=0.017). Limitations include reliance on self-report questionnaires and correlational (non-causal) interpretation, with no ML modeling or ILSA PV framework involved.
